name: What carried Bantu languages across a third of Africa?

positions.claim: Bantu-speaking farmers moved fastest through environments like the ones they knew, and a climate crisis about 2,500 years ago opened a savanna corridor through the rainforest.
positions.mech: Climate fragmented the forest; farmers tracked savanna and paused at forest edges.
for: A phylogeny of more than 400 Bantu languages mapped on vegetation shows speed changing with habitat (Grollemund et al. 2015).
Pollen cores and site dates cluster after the Late Holocene rainforest crisis (Bostoen et al. 2015).
against: Some groups were in the forest centuries before the crisis, along rivers and coasts.
Phylogenies depend on how the language tree is rooted and sampled.

positions.claim: An expansion of farming communities, later armed with iron tools and with grains and cattle borrowed from neighbours, spread Bantu languages east and south.
positions.mech: Demographic growth of farmers over foragers, sped up by iron and new crops.
for: Loanwords for cattle, grains and ironworking trace contact with Sudanic and Cushitic speakers (Ehret 1998).
Early Iron Age pottery traditions spread fast from the Great Lakes to southern Africa (Phillipson).
against: The western spread began before iron.
Words and pots can move without many people moving.

positions.claim: There was no Bantu "expansion" in the sense of a migration wave, but thousands of small moves and language shifts over millennia, carrying institutions as well as words.
positions.mech: Gradual drift and adoption of languages and political traditions.
for: The equatorial political vocabulary (house, village, district) is shared and old (Vansina 1990).
Linguistic subgroups do not line up with one wave (Vansina 1995).
against: Genetics now show large-scale movement of people, not just words (Patin et al. 2017).

positions.claim: Genomes confirm a real movement of people from West-Central Africa, who mixed with foragers and herders; eastern and southern speakers split off late, after crossing the forest.
positions.mech: Demic diffusion with admixture along a route through the rainforest.
for: Genome-wide data from many African populations support a late split (Patin et al. 2017).
A Bayesian phylogeography favours a rainforest route (Koile et al. 2022).
against: Living genomes are blurred by later movements; ancient DNA from Central Africa is still scarce.

state: The field agrees on a real, mostly demic expansion from the Nigeria-Cameroon borderlands starting about 5,000 years ago, with heavy mixing along the way. It argues over the route (through the forest or around it), the timing of the eastern split, and how much climate and iron set the pace.
settle: Ancient DNA from Central African forest sites, and more securely dated early village sites south of the forest, would fix the route and timing.
fun: A drought 2,500 years ago may have opened the door that let one language family cover a third of a continent.

name: Who built Great Zimbabwe, what made it rich, and why did it fade?

positions.claim: Phoenicians, Sabaeans or Arabs built the ruins; Africans were labourers or later squatters.
positions.mech: Diffusionist racism: complex building assumed impossible for Africans.
for: Imported glass, porcelain and coins at the site showed long-distance trade.
against: Every dated layer and artefact is African; the architecture and pottery belong to Shona-speaking ancestors (Randall-MacIver 1906, Caton-Thompson 1931).
The theory served settler politics and was kept alive by censorship.

positions.school: A Shona state built on gold and ivory
positions.claim: Ancestors of the Shona built Great Zimbabwe as the capital of a state that grew rich controlling gold and ivory sent to the Swahili coast; it faded when trade moved north and local resources ran down.
positions.mech: Tribute and trade wealth concentrated in a sacred elite, which built in stone.
for: Imports at the site match Kilwa and Sofala trade goods.
The sequence from Mapungubwe to Great Zimbabwe to Khami shows continuity (Huffman 2009).
against: Gold-working and gold finds at the site itself are modest.
Trade alone does not explain the scale of building.

positions.claim: The everyday basis of power was cattle, and seasonal transhumance explains the site’s position between highveld and lowveld.
positions.mech: Herds as wealth and patronage.
for: Cattle bones dominate the faunal remains.
against: Cattle were wealth across the region, but only some places became capitals.

positions.school: A longer, more complex African past
positions.claim: New dating shows Great Zimbabwe was built and lived in over a longer span and in a different order than once thought, and that its story was confiscated by colonial science.
positions.mech: Re-dating a vandalised site and decolonising its interpretation.
for: Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates re-threads the building sequence (Chirikure et al. 2013).
against: Hall’s clearance destroyed much of the stratigraphy any model needs.

state: African origin has been settled since 1905 and is beyond dispute. The live arguments are about the chronology, the balance of trade and cattle in the economy, how far Huffman’s structuralist reading of the space holds, and how sudden the decline was.
settle: More dates from intact deposits on the Hill and in the valley, and isotopic work on cattle and people, would settle chronology and economy.
fun: For eighty years white governments insisted Africans could not have built it; the country now carries its name.

name: What made Mali rich and powerful: Saharan gold, Islam, or older Niger towns?

positions.claim: Mali controlled the passage of gold from the Bambuk and Bure fields to the Saharan caravans and grew rich on taxes and trade.
positions.mech: Taxing a choke point between goldfields and desert ports.
for: Arabic writers stress gold above all (Levtzion and Hopkins 1981).
Musa’s hajj spent enough gold to move Cairo’s prices.
against: Mansas did not directly run the goldfields; miners kept their autonomy.
The written sources are North African and see Mali through trade.

positions.claim: Mali was a political creation of the Mande: Sunjata’s coalition, a military aristocracy and a court that used Islam and spectacle to gain standing in the wider world.
positions.mech: Coalition-building, cavalry and religious diplomacy.
for: The Sunjata tradition and the Kurukan Fuga charter describe a federal order.
The hajj and Timbuktu’s mosques were deliberate statecraft.
against: Oral epics were shaped by later griots and kings.

positions.claim: Jenne-jeno and other Middle Niger towns had urban life and regional trade from about 250 BCE, so the Saharan trade grafted onto an African network rather than creating it.
positions.mech: Heterarchical urbanism and regional specialisation.
for: Excavations at Jenne-jeno show iron, copper and trade goods long before Arab contact (McIntosh and McIntosh 1981).
against: Early towns explain commerce, not the scale of Mali’s empire.

positions.school: West Africa in a global gold economy
positions.claim: West African gold underpinned Mediterranean and European coinage, so European shortages and Portuguese ships reshaped where the gold went and who profited.
positions.mech: Demand from outside pulled the trade, and Atlantic routes later diverted it.
for: The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows how famous Mali’s gold was in Europe.
Europe’s fifteenth-century bullion famine (Day 1978) coincides with Portuguese voyages.
against: Hard to measure the gold flows; diversion to the coast came after Mali’s peak.

state: Most historians now combine gold and statecraft: Mali needed the gold trade, but its power came from Mande political organisation and its savvy use of Islam. The global angle is growing.
settle: More excavation at Mali’s capitals (the site of Niani is disputed) and better provenance of medieval gold coins would show where wealth and power sat.
fun: A king spent so much gold on his way to Mecca that he crashed the price of gold in Cairo for years.

name: How many Africans were carried across the Atlantic?

positions.claim: About 9.6 million Africans were landed in the Americas.
positions.mech: Compiled published import estimates and shipping data.
for: The first systematic count, and within about 10 percent of later landed figures.
against: Undercounted the Portuguese and Brazilian trade.

positions.claim: Curtin missed many voyages; the real number shipped was well above his, perhaps 15 million.
positions.mech: Correcting for undercounted British and Portuguese shipping.
for: Archival work found voyages missing from Curtin.
against: The voyage database, with most voyages now documented, comes in lower.

positions.claim: Combining the revisions gives close to 12 million exported from Africa.
positions.mech: Synthesising regional studies.
for: Close to the later database totals.
against: Built on aggregates rather than voyage records.

positions.claim: About 12.5 million people embarked and about 10.7 million landed; the trade peaked in the late eighteenth century.
positions.mech: Voyage-by-voyage records for some 36,000 voyages, with imputation for gaps.
for: Most voyages are documented individually and open online.
against: Imputation for undocumented voyages is still a model.

positions.claim: The records are too thin to support precise numbers or the demographic conclusions drawn from them.
positions.mech: Source criticism of the evidence behind each estimate.
for: Many early voyages and the African side of the trade are poorly documented.
against: The database has narrowed uncertainty far more than critics expected.

state: The voyage database has largely settled the order of magnitude: about 12.5 million embarked, 10.7 million landed. Argument continues over the sixteenth century, the Portuguese-Brazilian trade, and deaths in Africa before embarkation, which no ship record counts.
settle: Portuguese and Brazilian archives for the early trade, and estimates of deaths inside Africa during capture and march to the coast.
fun: One ship log at a time, historians rebuilt 36,000 voyages and turned a guess into a count.

name: What did the Atlantic slave trade do to Africa?

positions.claim: The trade drained Africa of labour, fed war, stunted manufacturing and helped build the industrial economies of the Atlantic: Europe developed as Africa was underdeveloped.
positions.mech: Unequal exchange of people for consumer goods and guns.
for: Guns and cloth were leading imports (Inikori 1977).
Upper Guinea coast case study (Rodney 1970).
against: African textile production remained large; imports were a small part of consumption (Thornton 1992).

positions.claim: African rulers and merchants controlled supply and sold captives from wars fought for their own reasons; Europeans could not force the trade.
positions.mech: African political economy decided who was enslaved and when.
for: Europeans held only coastal forts at Africans’ pleasure.
Kongo’s and Dahomey’s wars had local political causes.
against: Agency at the top does not mean benefit for the many who were captured.

positions.claim: Population in the main exporting regions stagnated or fell between 1730 and 1850, and Africa’s share of world population dropped.
positions.mech: Losses of young adults outran births.
for: Manning’s demographic simulations.
against: African population data before 1900 are extremely thin.

positions.claim: The export trade turned slavery inside Africa from a marginal status into a central mode of production that grew even after the Atlantic trade ended.
positions.mech: Institutions built for export turned inward.
for: Nineteenth-century Sokoto and the palm oil economies used huge numbers of slaves.
against: Slavery existed in many African societies before the Atlantic trade.

positions.claim: Regions that lost more people to the slave trades are poorer today, and people from more raided groups trust others less.
positions.mech: Raiding broke states into fragments and made mistrust a cultural norm.
for: Cross-country regressions on 52 countries (Nunn 2008).
Afrobarometer trust data by ethnic group (Nunn and Wantchekon 2011).
against: Ethnic export counts rest on shipping records of uncertain coverage.
Climate and other shocks also moved exports (Fenske and Kala 2015).

state: Few now defend the minimal-impact view. The field agrees the trade cost Africa population and security; it argues over how much of today’s poverty runs through the slave trades rather than colonialism and later events.
settle: Better reconstructions of African population before 1900, and tests of the persistence results on independent local data.
fun: Economists found that the more slaves a region lost two centuries ago, the less its people trust their neighbours today.

name: Why did Europe carve up Africa in about thirty years?

positions.claim: Underconsumption and the rise of finance capital pushed investors to seek returns abroad and governments to secure colonies.
positions.mech: Capital export needed political control.
for: British capital exports soared after 1870.
against: Very little went to tropical Africa; colonies were mostly a net cost to taxpayers (Davis and Huttenback 1986).

positions.school: The official mind and the Egyptian trigger
positions.claim: Statesmen acted to protect strategic routes, above all to India; the occupation of Egypt in 1882, forced by a local crisis, set off a chain reaction.
positions.mech: Peripheral crises drew reluctant governments into formal rule.
for: Cabinet papers show strategic, not commercial, reasoning.
against: Hopkins (1986) showed financial interests in Egypt were large and well connected.

positions.claim: Falling commodity prices strained West African trade, and London’s financial elite pressed for protection of bondholders and markets, as in Egypt.
positions.mech: Commercial and financial pressure on the metropole.
for: The palm oil price slump and merchant lobbying (Hopkins 1973).
against: Timing of annexations does not always follow prices.

positions.claim: Quinine, steamers, breech-loaders and machine guns made conquest cheap; they explain when, not why.
positions.mech: Technology lowered the cost of conquest.
for: European death rates in West Africa fell sharply after quinine (Curtin 1989).
Omdurman.
against: African states also acquired modern rifles, as Adwa showed.

positions.claim: African states fought, negotiated and allied, shaping where and how conquest happened, and the borders and violence still shape Africa.
positions.mech: African politics and resistance set the pace and form.
for: Samori, Adwa and Maji Maji.
Partitioned homelands see more conflict today (Michalopoulos and Papaioannou 2016).
against: Resistance usually failed militarily; the decisions were made in Europe.

state: Most historians now see several causes working together: strategic rivalry triggered by Egypt, commercial crisis in West Africa, cheap conquest thanks to new technology, and African politics shaping the outcome. Hobson and Lenin are read more as critics of their age than as explanations.
settle: Comparative studies of each annexation’s timing against prices, strategy and the lobbying record.
fun: In 1880 most of Africa was ruled by Africans; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were not under European rule.

name: Why did the enslaved of Saint-Domingue win, and what kind of revolution was it?

positions.claim: A revolution of the enslaved masses, inspired and opened by the French Revolution and led by Toussaint Louverture, part of the Atlantic age of revolution.
positions.mech: Class struggle meeting revolutionary ideas.
for: Toussaint’s letters use the language of the Republic.
against: Underplays African-born insurgents and their own political ideas.

positions.claim: The masses, organised through maroon bands and Vodou, drove the revolution and often pushed past their leaders.
positions.mech: Popular mobilisation and maroon traditions.
for: Local studies of the South and the plantations.
against: Evidence on pre-1791 maroon networks is thin.

positions.claim: Most insurgents were African-born, many from Kongo with military experience and royalist ideas of legitimate rule.
positions.mech: African military skill and political ideology.
for: Insurgent leaders’ royalist rhetoric; Kongolese names and tactics (Thornton 1993).
against: Leadership came largely from the creole elite.

positions.school: Universal rights made in the Caribbean
positions.claim: Insurgents forced French officials to free them in 1793 and the Republic to abolish slavery in 1794; when Napoleon brought slavery back, they won independence.
positions.mech: Contingent wartime emancipation expanded the meaning of rights.
for: Sonthonax’s 1793 decree came from military need.
Independence followed news of re-enslavement in Guadeloupe.
against: Puts weight on French decisions, not only on the insurgents.

positions.claim: Yellow fever destroyed Leclerc’s army, while the insurgents were largely immune.
positions.mech: Differential immunity.
for: Most of the expedition’s soldiers died of disease, including Leclerc.
against: Fever needed an army that could hold out through the season, which the insurgents had.

positions.claim: The revolution was unthinkable to contemporaries and then written out of history; Haiti was punished with isolation and a crushing indemnity.
positions.mech: Power shapes what history remembers.
for: The 1825 indemnity and decades of non-recognition.
against: Haiti’s revolution was widely discussed at the time, in fear.

state: Historians now see a revolution made largely by African-born insurgents, shaped by African and French ideas, which forced the first general abolition and the first Black republic. Disease and French politics mattered, but as conditions the insurgents exploited.
settle: More work in African-language and Kreyol sources and in Spanish and British archives on insurgent politics.
fun: Half a million enslaved people defeated three empires and the world never quite forgave them.

name: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492, and what killed nine in ten of them?

positions.claim: Ninety to 112 million people lived in the Americas, 25 million in central Mexico alone; epidemics ran ahead of Europeans and erased whole societies before anyone wrote them down.
positions.mech: Back-projection from early colonial counts using depopulation ratios.
for: Colonial tribute counts show a 90 percent fall in central Mexico (Cook and Borah).
against: Depopulation ratios are guesses; early counts are padded (Henige 1998).

positions.claim: The high counts multiply unreliable sources by arbitrary ratios; north of Mexico, the evidence supports a couple of million.
positions.mech: Source criticism and skeletal and archaeological estimates.
for: Chroniclers’ figures are rhetorical and inflated.
against: Archaeology keeps finding dense populations (Amazonian earthworks, LiDAR).

positions.claim: About 50 to 60 million people, with a fall of around 90 percent by 1600.
positions.mech: Region-by-region estimates combined.
for: Koch et al. (2019) combine published regional estimates.
Landscapes were heavily managed (Denevan 1992).
against: Wide ranges in every region.

positions.claim: Old World diseases struck populations with no prior exposure, and that alone explains most deaths.
positions.mech: Lack of acquired immunity.
for: Smallpox in 1520 and cocoliztli in 1545 and 1576.
Salmonella DNA in cocoliztli victims (Vågene et al. 2018).
against: Epidemics kill far more when people are enslaved, starving and displaced (Jones 2003).

positions.claim: Conquest made disease deadly: forced labour, enslavement, famine and war crushed births and multiplied deaths; Hispaniola’s Taíno were collapsing before smallpox arrived.
positions.mech: Colonial violence set the conditions for epidemic mortality.
for: Hispaniola’s numbers fell before 1518 (Livi Bacci 2003).
The Native slave trade preceded the Southeast’s great epidemic (Kelton 2007).
against: In central Mexico the 1520 epidemic struck before Spanish rule took hold.

positions.school: The Great Dying changed the climate
positions.claim: So many deaths let about 56 million hectares regrow, pulling CO2 down by 7 to 10 ppm by 1610 and nudging the Little Ice Age colder.
positions.mech: Reforestation as a carbon sink.
for: Law Dome ice cores show the 1610 dip.
against: The cooling effect is small next to solar and volcanic forcing; other carbon sinks are possible.

state: Most scholars accept a pre-contact population in the tens of millions and a collapse of around 90 percent in a century. They now see disease and colonial violence working together rather than as rivals. The climate effect is accepted as real but small.
settle: Systematic archaeology of settlement density (LiDAR, ancient DNA) and pathogen genomes from more epidemic victims.
fun: So many people died after 1492 that the forests grew back and the air itself lost carbon.

name: How did a few hundred Spaniards topple the Aztec and Inca empires?

positions.claim: Steel, horses, guns and above all epidemic disease gave Europeans an advantage rooted in Eurasian geography.
positions.mech: Technological and epidemiological gaps.
for: Smallpox killed Cuitlahuac and Huayna Capac.
Cajamarca: 168 Spaniards seized the Inca.
against: Spaniards always fought alongside huge Indigenous armies.

positions.school: Indigenous allies and a fragile hegemony
positions.claim: The conquest of Mexico was largely an Indigenous war: Tlaxcala and other altepetl used the Spaniards to destroy Mexica dominance.
positions.mech: Hegemonic empire with resentful tributaries and unconquered enemies.
for: Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans at the siege; Indigenous conquistadors in later campaigns.
against: Allies would not have turned without Spanish successes and epidemic shock.

positions.claim: The godlike Cortés, the fatalistic Moctezuma and the idea of a quick conquest are later inventions; Nahuatl sources show calculating Indigenous politics.
positions.mech: Reading Spanish and Nahua sources against the grain.
for: Nahuatl annals and the accounts in The Broken Spears.
against: Some Spanish eyewitness sources are early and specific.

positions.claim: An epidemic killed Huayna Capac and his heir, the succession war split the empire, and Pizarro seized the victor; recently conquered Andean peoples backed the Spaniards.
positions.mech: Succession crisis plus disease plus allies.
for: Sarmiento and other chronicles of the Huascar-Atahualpa war.
against: Chronicles were written for Spanish purposes.

positions.claim: Conquest was a long process of negotiation, resistance and adaptation; Nahua city-states and Andean communities survived and reshaped colonial rule.
positions.mech: Indigenous institutions persisted under new masters.
for: Nahuatl documents from the altepetl (Lockhart 1992).
Vilcabamba until 1572; Taki Onqoy.
against: Survival of institutions coexisted with demographic catastrophe.

state: The New Conquest History has made Indigenous allies, Indigenous sources and epidemic disease central, and treats the triumphalist story as myth. Diamond’s technology argument survives only as one factor among several.
settle: More Nahuatl, Quechua and colonial litigation sources on how allied communities chose sides.
fun: The Aztec capital fell to an army that was mostly Indigenous; the Spaniards were its smallest contingent.

name: Did Potosí’s silver make the first global economy, and at what cost?

positions.school: American treasure and the price revolution
positions.claim: Treasure imports raised Spanish and then European prices.
positions.mech: Quantity theory of money.
for: Spanish prices and treasure imports rise together (Hamilton 1934).
against: Prices rose before big silver imports; much silver passed through to Asia.

positions.claim: Population growth and urbanisation drove inflation; silver accommodated it.
positions.mech: Demand for food outran supply; faster circulation of money in towns.
for: English prices rose with population before silver arrived (Goldstone 1984).
against: Silver still mattered for the level of prices in Spain.

positions.claim: Ming China, taxing in silver, valued it far above Europe, and its demand pulled American and Japanese silver round the world: global trade began in 1571 at Manila.
positions.mech: Arbitrage between silver prices in China and the Americas.
for: Gold-silver ratios in China around half Europe’s.
The Manila galleon from 1571.
against: How much silver reached China and whether a fall in imports helped bring down the Ming are disputed (Atwell vs von Glahn).

positions.claim: The boom rested on the mita draft and mercury, which killed and poisoned Andean workers and left a measurable poverty gap today.
positions.mech: Coerced cheap labour and toxic refining.
for: About 13,000 men drafted yearly; Huancavelica’s mortality; Dell’s boundary design.
against: Many workers were wage-earners (mingas) and some Indigenous people grew rich.

positions.claim: The first boom ran on Andean smelting technology, Andean workers and Andean markets.
positions.mech: Guayra wind furnaces and wage labour.
for: Cieza’s eyewitness account of guayras and the Potosí market.
against: After 1572 Spanish amalgamation and coercion dominated.

state: Global historians agree Potosí silver tied the Americas, Europe and China together, and that the mita was its brutal engine. The price revolution is now usually explained by population growth as well as silver, and the Ming silver crisis remains disputed.
settle: Better series of silver arriving in China and of prices across Eurasia.
fun: A single mountain in the Andes paid for Spain’s wars and China’s taxes, and the villages that mined it are still poorer.

name: Why did the Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands collapse?

positions.claim: A series of severe multi-year droughts between about 760 and 910 broke the farming and water systems of the southern lowlands.
positions.mech: Rainfall failure on societies dependent on stored rainwater.
for: Lake Chichancanab and Cariaco Basin sediments; Belize stalagmite (Kennett 2012).
against: Collapse was uneven and began in places (Petexbatún) before the worst droughts; the wetter north did not suffer equally.

positions.claim: Population outgrew the land: deforestation and erosion left no buffer when drought came.
positions.mech: Ecological overshoot.
for: Erosion layers in lakes; LiDAR shows dense farms and terraces (Canuto 2018).
against: Many Maya landscapes were well managed for centuries.

positions.claim: Competitive divine kingship, endless war and elite excess undermined itself.
positions.mech: Political ideology failed; commoners withdrew support.
for: Petexbatún wars from the 760s; end of dated monuments.
against: Political failure needs a trigger, and climate fits the timing.

positions.claim: Southern kingship ended but Maya society reorganised in the north and on the coasts; millions of Maya live today.
positions.mech: Resilience and reorganisation.
for: Chichen Itza and the northern lowlands flourished; Terminal Classic variation (Aimers 2007).
against: The southern population loss was still enormous.

state: A synthesis is emerging: drought was the trigger, acting on dense, politically fragile kingdoms already at war, and what collapsed was a political system rather than a people.
settle: More finely dated local climate records matched site by site to the end of building and occupation.
fun: A drop in rainfall of maybe a quarter was enough to end a civilisation of kings, but not its people.
